translations.text: Discourse of our holy father Basil on the saying of the Gospel of Luke, which speaks about the rich man, that:
"I will pull down my storehouses and build greater ones," and on greed.
Trials take two forms: for either afflictions come to test the heart, as gold is tested in fire,
and through patience they reveal its goodness; or else the delights of this world become a trial for many.
For it is equally difficult to keep the soul unwounded in hard circumstances and, when in glory, not to grow arrogant and turn to wickedness.
Of the first kind of trial, the example is the great Job, that invincible contender, who met all the warfare of the devil, like the violence of a river,
with an unshaken heart and an untroubled mind; and the greater and more overwhelming the trials the enemy thought he was bringing upon him, the more he rose above them all.
But of the trials that come from the delights of the world there are many other examples as well:
and one of them is this rich man about whom we have just read, who had some wealth already and was expecting more,
since God, the lover of humankind, did not from the first condemn him for his foolish mind,
but continually gave him wealth upon wealth, so that he might at some point satisfy him and in this way bring his soul to generosity and to giving to others.
That is why it says: "The land of a certain rich man was fruitful, and he thought within himself: What shall I do?
I will pull down my storehouses and build greater ones."
But why did the land of that man become fruitful, when he was not going to do a single good thing with its fruitfulness?
Only for this reason: that the long-suffering of God might be shown the more, how his goodness reaches even to such people as these, for:
He rains on the righteous and on sinners, and makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good.
But this goodness of his brings a greater judgment upon the wicked, for he brought rain on the land plowed by those greedy hands;
he gave the sun for that seed to sprout and for the fruits to multiply many times over. And such are the works of God:
the goodness of the earth, the well-tempered conditions of the air, the abundance of the seed, the help of the oxen, and the other things by which labor is made fruitful.
But let us see, what in turn are the deeds of that man?
Bitterness of mind, hatred of his fellow men, mercilessness. This is what he did in return to his benefactor:
he did not remember the nature we share, he did not see fit to give his surplus to the poor, and he counted as nothing at all the commandment which says:
"Do not neglect to do good to the needy," and: "Let not mercy and faith fail you," and: "Break your bread for the hungry."
And all the prophets and teachers cried out, and he did not listen to them; instead his storehouses were bursting, strained by the great quantity of what lay in them.
Yet that greedy heart was not satisfied, for he kept adding the new to the old, and year by year he multiplied his wealth by these additions;
And so he fell into this tight and helpless strait, for out of greed he could not bear to part with the old grain, and he had not enough room to take in the new because of its abundance.
Therefore his plans could not be carried out and his cares had no end, for he said: "What shall I do?"
Who would not pity such a man, so taken captive?
He is wretched because of his fruitfulness, pitiable because of the good things he has, and more pitiable still because of those that are to come.
The earth does not bring him fruit so much as it sprouts sighs for him;
he does not gather wealth, but cares and griefs and terrible helplessness; he laments just as the poor do.
Does not the man hard pressed by poverty say this very same thing: "What shall I do?
Where shall I get food or clothing?" So too the rich man says it, while his heart burns and he is consumed by care.
For what gladdens others wears away the greedy man, for he does not rejoice that all his storehouses are full,
but the increase and overflow of wealth, spilling over from the storehouses, stings his soul.
He is distressed lest the overflow should reach those outside and become a source of some good to the needy.
And this affliction of his soul, as I think, is like that of gluttons, who would rather burst from eating than give their leftovers to the poor.
Consider the Giver, O man. Remember yourself: who you are, what you are steward of, from whom you have received it, and why you were made more honored than others.

You are a servant of the good God, a steward over your fellow servants. Do not wish to store up everything for your own belly; take thought for what is in your hands as for things belonging to others.
For a little time they will gladden you, and then they will flow away from you and be gone, but a strict account of them will be demanded of you.
But you have shut everything up behind doors and bolts, and you hold it and have secured it with seals,
and you lie awake with care for these things and deliberate within yourself, taking counsel with a foolish counselor, yourself, saying: "What shall I do?"
You ought to have said: "I will fill the souls of the poor; I will open my storehouses and call the needy.
I will be like Joseph in that proclamation of love for humankind; I will send out the voice of mercy, saying:
'All you who lack bread, come to me, and from this grace given by God, as from a common spring, let each of you draw what he needs.'"
But you are not like this. Why? Because you begrudge people, lest they find relief through you.
Instead you have devised an evil plan in your soul, and you take care not for how you may give each one what he needs,
but for how you may take everything and shut everyone out from any benefit of it, as that rich man did.
Those who carry off the soul stood by, and he was speaking to his soul about food.
That very night his soul was being taken from him, and he was dreaming of the pleasure of many years.
He was permitted to deliberate on everything according to his own will and to reveal his mind, and so to receive a sentence worthy of his will,
which may it not come upon you; for this is why it was written, so that we might flee from becoming like him.
Be like the earth, O man; you too bring forth fruit as it brings forth; do not become worse than that lifeless thing.
For it brings forth fruits not for its own rest, but for your service;
but you, whatever fruit of good works you produce, you gather it for yourself, for the favors of good deeds go back to those who give.
If you give to the hungry, what you have given is truly yours, for it will come back to you in greater abundance.
As wheat sown in the earth becomes a profit to the sower, so also bread given to the hungry will afterward yield its profit many times over.
Let the end of your labor, then, be for you the beginning of that eternal sowing in the heavens, for it is written: "Sow for yourselves unto righteousness."
Why, then, are you at a loss? Why do you waste yourself away with care and hurry to shut up your wealth in clay and brick?
"A good name is better than great riches." But if you love wealth for the honor that comes from it, consider
how much better it is for your glory to be called the father of myriads of the poor than to have myriads of gold in treasuries.
For your goods, even if you do not wish it, you will leave here, but for your good deeds you will receive honor before the King,
when the assembly of the poor whom you have fed surrounds you before the Judge of all, and they name you nourisher and benefactor and call you by every name of love for mankind.
Do you not see at the spectacles those singers and mimes and men who fight beasts, whose doings are loathsome even to watch,
how for that small and worthless honor, and for a great volume of praise, they squander their wealth?
But you are feeble and grudging about spending money, you who are destined to enter into such glory.

For God will be the one who approves your deed, and the angels will praise you, and all people from the beginning will call you blessed; eternal glory will be given to you, the crown of righteousness, the kingdom of heaven.
All this will be in exchange for giving away this perishable money; yet for none of these things do you care, and in your eagerness over present things you disregard the hope of things to come.
Come, then, and distribute that wealth in various ways, and be an honorable and good giver to the needy, so that it may be said of you too:
"He scattered and gave it to the poor, and his righteousness endures forever." Do not raise the price at the time of pressing need.
Do not wait for famine, so that only then you open your treasuries and acquire money by selling what is in them.
Do not long for famine for the sake of gold, or for the want of all people for the sake of your own enrichment.
Do not become a trafficker in the calamities of men; do not make the time of God's wrath a time for acquiring goods.
Do not add to the wound of the hungry another wound by raising the price.
But you look at gold and do not look at your brother. You recognize the inscribed drachma and distinguish untested gold from tested, but of your hungry brother you are wholly ignorant.
The color of the gold draws you, and you do not consider how many sighs of the poor man follow after you.
How can I set before your eyes the suffering and distress of the poor man?
He examines the inside of his house and sees that he has no gold and expects none from anywhere,
while his clothes and vessels are such as those of the poor usually are, all worth only a few small coins.
So he seeks some means of escaping death by hunger.
Finding no other means, he looks to his own children, to take them to be sold and so find relief from death.
At this point consider the turmoil between the distress of hunger and the nature of parenthood.
The one side threatens him with an evil death, while on the other side his mind draws him to die together with his children.
And after he has been worn down many times, he is at last overcome, hard pressed by inescapable need.
And what must that father's deliberation be! For he says: "Which one shall I sell first?
Or which would the wheat seller more readily accept? Shall I go to the eldest?
But I am ashamed before his seniority. Shall I sell the youngest, then?
But I pity his tender age, which is still unacquainted with trials.
This one clearly bears the likeness of his parents before his eyes; that one, again, is good at learning.
O, what shall I do in these hopeless trials? Against which of these shall I offend? What wild beast's soul shall I take on?
How shall I forget my own nature? If I spare them all, I shall see them all perish miserably from hunger.
If I sell one, with what eyes shall I look at the others, since I shall be suspect and untrustworthy to them?
How shall I dwell in a house in which I have brought the trial of childlessness upon my own head?
How shall I sit down at a table spread for such a reason?"
And so he comes with many tears to sell his beloved child, yet that suffering does not move you, and you take no account of nature.
Hunger has seized that wretched man and is choking him, while you delay and act disdainfully, and prolong the trial upon him.
He gives you his own bowels and loins as the price of food, yet your hand not only does not go numb at taking payment from such trials,
but you haggle for more and dispute, so as to receive more and give little. In every way you make the trials heavier for that pitiable man.
Neither do tears seem pitiable to you, nor do sighs move your heart, but you are unbending and merciless.
On every side you see only gold; gold appears to you in your fancies. It is your dream when you sleep and your preoccupation when you are awake.
Like those who have been robbed of their wits by a demon, who do not see things as they are but see the fantasies of their passion,
so too your soul is gripped by the love of gold, and you see everything as gold, everything as silver.
You fix your eyes on gold with more delight than on the sun. You pray that everything might be changed into the nature of gold, and you do just that, as far as you are able.
For what scheme do you not set in motion for the sake of gold?
Wheat becomes gold for you, you freeze wine into gold, wool is changed by you into gold; every trade, every scheme brings you gold.
Gold itself begets itself for you and through you, when it multiplies by lending and interest.
And there is no satiety, and no end to that desire is found.
For we often give gluttonous children more than they need, so that through excess of satiety they may turn away from it,
but greed is not like this; rather, the more it receives, the more it longs for still more. "If riches overflow, do not set your hearts on them."
But you hold back that river and block its outlets, and then see what it will do to you through that holding back and damming: it will break through the dividing wall and the barriers.
Just as, behold, you hear about that rich man, how he too wished to act in this way, and how that wealth was held back by force and compulsion and was overflowing.
And what is going to happen? It will tear down the rich man's storehouses and lay waste his treasuries, like some enemy who has come upon them. But perhaps he will build larger ones?
I do not know whether he would not have left them torn down to those who came after him, for he departed, snatched away, sooner than they could have been built according to the mind of his greed.
But he received an end befitting that evil plan.
But as for you, if you believe me, open wide all the doors of your treasuries and give your wealth an outlet without grudging.
As a great river flows in many directions over fruitful land, so you too must give your wealth a way to go in many directions to the houses of the poor.
For springs too, when they are drawn from, well up all the more, but when left alone they go bad.
And wealth laid away is useless, but that which is emptied out and given to the poor is fruitful.
Oh, how great will be the praise of the poor upon you, which you must not despise, and how great will be your reward from that righteous Judge, whom you must not disbelieve!

And may the example of this rich man come to your mind always, who guarded what was in his hands and was anxious about what was to come, not knowing whether he would exist until tomorrow, and who was committing tomorrow's sin already today:
The servant had not yet come, and he was already showing cruelty; he had not yet gathered the fruit, and he already had the condemnation for greed.
The land displayed its fruitfulness to him, for it richly brought up the standing grain, and large clusters appeared on the vine,
and the olive tree brought forth fruit in overflowing measure, and every good thing from the trees was in abundance.
But he was wicked and unfruitful: he did not yet have it, and already he was begrudging the poor. And how many things happen before the fruits are gathered?
For often hail shatters it, and scorching heat destroys it, and rain coming out of season ruins it.
And you, O rich man, will you not pray to the Lord that he may bring that grace to completion? Instead you rush ahead and make yourself unworthy of receiving the fruit that has appeared.
And you speak to yourself in secret, but your words are judged in the heavens; therefore the answer to your thoughts comes from there.
But hear also the words of the rich man: "Soul, you have many good things, stored up for many years; eat and drink and enjoy yourself every day."
O this brutishness! Even if you had the soul of pigs and not of human beings, what greater word of good news could you have given it?
So like the beasts you are, so without understanding of the good things of the soul, that you entertain it with bodily food, and what goes out into the drain, that you give to the soul as a gift.
If it has virtue and is full of good works and is united to God, then truly it has good things, and let it rejoice with that good joy of the soul.
But since you think on earthly things and have your belly for a god and are wholly fleshly, enslaved to the passions,
hear the name that befits you, the one by which no human being called you, but the Lord himself, that is:
"Fool, this night they will take your soul from you; and what you have prepared, whose will it be?"
Worse than eternal torment is the laughter at his madness and the scorn.
For he who was to be snatched away after a little while, see what he plans, saying: "I will pull down my storehouses and build greater ones."
But I would say to him: You do well, for you are pulling them down, and those storehouses of iniquity deserve to be pulled down.
Lay waste with your own hands what you built wickedly; dismantle those granaries from which no one has received consolation.
Make that whole house, the guardian of greed, disappear. Tear off the roofs and take apart the walls, show that rotted wheat to the sun,
bring that bound wealth out of prison, expose those dark hidden hoards of Mammon.
"I will pull down my storehouses and build greater ones." And if you fill those too, what will you do then?
Or will you pull down again and build again? And what could be worse than this: endless toil, hurried building and then hasty pulling down again?
Have storehouses, if you wish: the bellies of the poor. Store up treasure for yourself in the heavens.
What you store there, neither moths will eat, nor will rot come upon it, nor will robbers snatch it away.
But you say: "I will give to the poor then, when I have filled the second storehouses too."
You have fixed long limits for your life. But see that the limit you do not know, but which God has set, does not overtake you first.
For that promise of yours is not a sign of goodness but of wickedness.
For you do not make the promise in order to give then, but in order to slip away now. Otherwise, what now prevents you from giving?
Is the poor man not [?] before you? Are the storehouses not full? Is the reward not ready? Is the commandment not shining clear?
Now the hungry man is dying, the naked man is freezing, the debtor is being strangled, and do you put off your mercy until tomorrow?
Hear what Solomon says: "Do not say, 'Go away and come back tomorrow and I will give to you,' for you do not know what tomorrow will bring."
Alas, what commandments you disregard! Because of your love of money you have stopped up your ears.
How much thanks you owed to the Benefactor! How you ought to have been radiant and rejoiced in that honor, that you do not go to another's doors to beg, but others come to yours.
But you are gloomy and hard to find; you flee from meeting the poor, lest you somehow be compelled to open your hand a little.
You have learned only one saying: "I do not have it, I will not give to you, for I am poor." Truly you are poor and lacking in every good thing:
poor in love, poor in love of humankind, poor in faith in God, poor in hope of eternal good things.
Wretched man, make your brothers sharers in your grain; what will rot tomorrow, give to the poor man today.
This is the evil and the utmost measure of greed, that you would not give to the poor even perishable things, which you yourself could not use.
But you say: "And what evil do I do in keeping what is mine?"
Tell me then, from where is all that yours? Where did you get it from and bring it into this world?

It is as if someone at a public spectacle were to see something worth seeing presented there, and were to prevent others from seeing it, and were to regard as his own what had been presented for all to see.
Such are the rich as well, for they have seized what was made for all and call that common property their own.
For if, as is right, each person took only what he needs for his use and left the rest to another, no one would be rich and no one poor.
Or did you not come out naked from your mother's womb? And will you not return naked to the earth again? So all this that you have, from where is it yours?
If you say that it comes from yourself, then you are godless, and you do not acknowledge the Creator or give thanks to the Giver.
But if you confess that it comes from God, tell us the reason: why was it given to you?
Is God perhaps unjust, since he did not divide this life equally among us? Or why are you rich and that man poor?
It is for this reason, beyond all doubt: that you may receive the reward of goodness and of faithful stewardship, and that he may be honored through the great struggles of patience.
But you have gathered everything into those insatiable bosoms of greed, and do you think that you harm no one, you who harm so many?
Who is greedy? He who does not stop at what is needed for use. And who is a robber? He who takes away what belongs to each person.
And are you not greedy? And are you not a robber, since you call your own what you received to manage and distribute?
Or if one who strips a clothed man is called a robber of men, is one who does not clothe the naked, when he has the power to do so, worthy of any other name?
The bread that you hold to no purpose belongs to the hungry and is not yours; the clothing that you have stored away in your treasuries belongs to the naked and is not yours;
The shoe that rots uselessly in your keeping belongs to the shoeless; the gold that you have buried belongs to the one in need and the destitute.
Now therefore know that you wrong as many people as you could have benefited.
"Those words are fine, but gold is better," you say, you who are blinded by greed, just as with those who speak of chastity to lovers of a harlot.
For the more someone denounces the harlot to them, the more they are inflamed to desire by the very mention of her.
But how shall I set before you the afflictions and struggles of the poor man, so that you may learn by what groans you are heaping up your treasure?
O how great a treasure will that word seem worth to you on the day of judgment, the word that says:
"Come, you blessed of my Father, and inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world, for I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink."
But what trembling and sweat and darkness will spread over you when you hear that sentence, which says:
"Depart from me, you cursed, into the outer darkness, which is prepared for the devil and his angels,
for I was hungry and you did not give me food, I was thirsty and you did not give me drink, I was naked and you did not clothe me."
For there not only the robber will be condemned, but also the merciless.
I, then, have said what I know to be better; and if you listen to me, the eternal good things that are to be given are evident.
But if you disobey me, the wrath to come stands written of itself; and I pray that you may be saved from tasting it,
when you put on a good mind, so that your wealth may become your ransom and you may attain the good things prepared in heaven, by the grace of him
who has called all people to his kingdom, to whom belong glory and might, now and always and forever and ever, amen.
